Bárbara

I have an answer to your first question regarding rqgam.check​.  That function has been revised in recent versions of the package and comes with this description in the details:

> Reproduces the "Resids vs. linear pred" plot from gam.check but using randomised quantile residuals...  Earlier versions of this function produced the full gam.check output, but this was confusing as only one of the plots was really useful. Checks of k are not computed, these need to be done using gam.check.

Therefore calling rqgam.check​ will only produce a single plot of residuals against the linear predictor.

Hello,

I was recently introduced to the distance package. I am working with avian and line transect data from 2012-2021. I keep getting this error message: "Error in check data(data, region.table, sample.table, obs.table, formula) : Region areas are not consistent.".  I changed all of my column names and doubled check if there were any discrepancies within my data.

I went even further and separated my data by year, and it worked perfectly. However, the dataset as a whole, I keep getting the error.  I can't figure out why I keep getting this message.

Thank you for your help in advance,

Eric Rexstad
Sat, Nov 13, 3:28 AM

Jelisa

It probably doesn't make much biological sense to analyze all four years together; the density estimates won't mean much.  Nevertheless, running everything in one swoop will smoke out some problems.

Your problem can be spotted with this line of code:
table(Grasslands$Region.Label, Grasslands$Area)

For two of your strata (Flying W L and Flying W North) they have two different areas recorded.  Digging a bit deeper

flyingwl <- subset(Grasslands, Region.Label=="Flying W L")
table(flyingwl$Area, flyingwl$Year)

          2012  2013  2019    2021
  793  100     79        0         328
  829    0         0       164          0

Sure enough, the acreage of this stratum was recorded as a different size in 2019.  Hence the complaint from the software about inconsistent region areas.  And the inconsistency disappears if you analyse the data year by year. I suspect you'll find a similar inconsistency for the Flying W North.

With a data set of this size, probably worthwhile to spend time doing simple sense-checks of the data such as these tables before trying to fit any detection functions.

messages.subject: Covered Area and NA Question
messages.body_plain:
Hi all. I am pretty new to Distance, so I apologize for these questions that probably should be obvious.

I did point count surveys (30 points, surveyed 1 to 3 times each in the same year) and recorded all birds seen at each point (so a multi-species dataset). For each bird detection I have region label, area (set to 0 to get density estimates only), sample label, effort, and distance. I want to account for the fact that most points were surveyed multiple times.

Ex:
Region, 0, point 1, 3, 20
Region, 0, point 1, 3, 15
Region, 0, point 2, 2, NA

First, I want to make sure that the points with NA are being imported properly because I get warnings saying "expecting numeric".

Second, I have several groups where I combined multiple species since I didn't have enough detections to analyze species individually. After analyzing all groups, I noticed that the "covered area" is different for all of them. Why is that? I assumed it had to do with different truncation distances for groups, but even the groups that have the same truncation distances have a different covered area. If I include all sample label and effort data for each observation and NAs, shouldn't the covered area be the same across groups?

Thanks so much for the help!

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Covered Area and NA Question
messages.body_plain:
Lianne

Welcome to the club.

The first question is pretty easy and is an R issue, not a distance sampling issue.  To get the NAs properly recognised, it matters what function you are using to read your data file.  For example, if you use read.table()​ there is an explicit argument for dealing with points without detections

read.table(file, header = FALSE, sep = "", quote = "\"'",
           dec = ".", numerals = c("allow.loss", "warn.loss", "no.loss"),
           row.names, col.names, as.is <http://as.is> = !stringsAsFactors,
           na.strings = "NA", colClasses = NA, nrows = -1,
           skip = 0, check.names = TRUE, fill = !blank.lines.skip,
           strip.white = FALSE, blank.lines.skip = TRUE,
           comment.char = "#",
           allowEscapes = FALSE, flush = FALSE,
           stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
           fileEncoding = "", encoding = "unknown", text, skipNul = FALSE)

that argument is na.strings​.  Other functions to read data will have something similar.

Your second question is somewhat more complex.  I suspect the problem lies not with the covered area​ but rather with the number of transects.  If there are points without detections for some species and not others, there will be a miscount of the number of points sampled.  Best solution to this issue is to explicitly tell the ds()​function about your survey design.  The arguments region.table​ and sample.table​ provide a way to let ds()​ know explicitly how many strata you have and their area (seems that you should know the size of your study area, no need to enter 0 for stratum size).  Likewise sample.table​ is used to indicate what points belong to what strata (and the number of times visited if they are points).

To demonstrate the problem, just this morning I worked up a small example, which I attach.  See if this explains your situation.

messages.body_plain:
Dan

Several questions for you:

By how much does detectability diminish from the centre of the photo to the edges?  Do you have a sense of that?  What is the size of the photo footprint on the ground (length and width)?  What do you know about the deterioration of detectability toward the edges of the images?  Is the deterioration symmetric (same detection top-to-bottom as from side-to-side?)

Often aerial photos are taken in sequence as an aircraft travels along the flight path.  It is not uncommon for the photos to be taken such that there is overlap of the images.  Combining the photos (taking account of frame overlap) is used to construct a transect of images.  The length of the overlaid images represents effort for a line transect distance sampling scenario.  The sampling unit is then the transect, of which there are presumably many to comprise a survey.

messages.body_plain:
Dan, an interesting problem.  If you expect detectability to fall off with distance from the centre, at all angles, then the method we used in this paper should work:

Summers, R.W. and Buckland, S.T. 2011.  A first survey of the global population size and distribution of the Scottish crossbill Loxia scotica.  Bird Conservation International 21, 186-198.

In that paper, the issue was that the species of interest occurred in forest, but much of the area around points was outside of forest.  Your problem should be easier, as you will know from geometry what the availability function is, without having to estimate it.  The method of allowing for decreased availability at greater distances is outlined in the following paper.

Buckland, S.T., Summers, R.W., Borchers, D.L. and Thomas, L. 2006.  Point transect sampling with traps or lures.  J. App. Ecol. 43, 377-384.

You’ll need to adapt the method to your problem, and unfortunately, this cannot be done in the Distance software, so would involve some programming, for example in R.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: Over-estimation of population densities
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I would like to update regarding my query, following my discussion with Eric so far. (Thanks Eric for your advice!)

While the results were still larger than the expected density/abundance, there were some advice and comments that Eric offered which were useful.
To check the number of detections per month before using the monthly data for analysis. The number of detections has to be sufficient in order to analyse the data month-by-month. If the number of monthly detections is sufficient, it is not necessary to use the pooled detection function. Using pooled detection function would invalidate the monthly estimates.
The data with which Eric has used to troubleshoot was for a hornbill species, which calls loudly. Negative exponential function would not be biologically feasible since the function gives a detectability model that falls away too quickly. This will result in an over-estimation of the figure as the model presumes that you detect only a small percentage of birds.
The effects of overlapping points do not affect the outcome significantly according to Buckland (2006) so it's not required to adjust for overlapping points.
Large flocks that occur very occasionally create large uncertainty to the average group size.
Buckland, S. T. (2006). Point transect surveys for songbirds: Robust methodologies. The Auk, 123(2), 345–357. https://doi.org/10.1093/auk/123.2.345

Regards,
Kah Ming
